{"new_lineages":[{"id":"L-c-extensions-easy","scope":"language","statement":"Python's implementation architecture made writing extension modules in C easy from the start."},{"id":"L-dynamic-loading","scope":"language","statement":"Python's import was interfaced with each platform's dynamic linking API so extension modules could be compiled and loaded separately as shared libraries, replacing early static linking into the interpreter and creating a cross-platform maintenance burden."},{"id":"L-distutils","scope":"language","statement":"The distutils tool let users build and install extension modules from anywhere and became a standard library module, but its complexity and lack of maintenance led to third-party alternatives and community fragmentation."},{"id":"L-embedding","scope":"language","statement":"Users asked for an embeddable Python, a library linkable into other applications, as Emacs embeds a Lisp interpreter."},{"id":"L-standalone-globals","scope":"other","statement":"Python was first conceived as a stand-alone program, so its C source freely defined global linker names without namespace discipline, which clashed with host applications when embedding."},{"id":"L-py-prefix","scope":"language","statement":"A naming convention was adopted prefixing all Python C globals with Py, _Py for internal names, and PY for macros, to avoid clashes."},{"id":"L-grand-renaming","scope":"method","statement":"The Py-prefix rename, a traumatic kind of event for developer communities, was done in two phases bridged by preprocessor macros for backwards compatibility, accompanied by adding unit tests to much of the standard library."},{"id":"L-functional-added","scope":"language","statement":"In January 1994 map(), filter(), reduce(), and the lambda operator for anonymous functions were added, a significant early chunk of contributed code."},{"id":"L-less-discussion-early","scope":"method","statement":"In the early days big changes required much less discussion than later, for better and worse."},{"id":"L-closures","scope":"language","statement":"Inner functions should implicitly carry references to the enclosing scope's referenced local variables (closures); lambda originally couldn't, needing default-argument workarounds, and closures were added in 2.1/2.2, proving useful for new-style classes and decorators."},{"id":"L-lambda-motivation","scope":"language","statement":"Users wanted a way to create anonymous functions in-line rather than defining a separate named function (as Lisp and Scheme allow), since Python had no such mechanism despite first-class functions, and the exec-string workaround was hacky."},{"id":"L-lambda-intent","scope":"language","statement":"Lambda was intended only as a syntactic tool for defining anonymous functions, not a full functional construct."},{"id":"L-lambda-terminology","scope":"language","statement":"The 'lambda' terminology, adopted for lack of a better alternative despite Van Rossum's unease, led functional-language users to expect semantics and advanced features Python lacked."},{"id":"L-not-functional","scope":"language","statement":"Van Rossum never viewed Python as a functional language or heavily influenced by them, and its dynamic nature rules out functional-style compile-time optimization such as tail recursion."},{"id":"L-functional-superseded","scope":"language","statement":"The map, filter, and reduce functions were largely superseded by list comprehensions and generator expressions; reduce was removed from the built-ins in Python 3 while lambda, map and filter stay."},{"id":"L-beaudry-hook","scope":"language","statement":"Don Beaudry's insight that custom kinds of class objects should be creatable led to a hook: a callable type used as a base class makes class creation call that type, letting C (and later Python via a __class__ attribute) extensions define class behavior; it felt like a hack because type objects weren't yet callable, and it seeded metaclasses and new-style classes."},{"id":"L-metaclass-namespace-limit","scope":"language","statement":"The class body is executed before the class creation function runs, so a metaclass could not influence the namespace the definitions run in; Python 3000 fixed this by letting a metaclass provide an alternative mapping, specified with keyword-argument syntax in the base-class list."},{"id":"L-class-creation-api","scope":"language","statement":"Defining a class executes its body in a local dictionary, then calls a class creation function with the name, a tuple of base classes, and that dictionary; originally internal, it became a public API and carried over unchanged into the Python 2.2 metaclass machinery."},{"id":"L-class-creation-hidden","scope":"language","statement":"In Python's original design classes were first-class objects, yet the act of creating a class was a fixed step hidden from users as an implementation detail."},{"id":"L-metaclass-no-syntax-change","scope":"language","statement":"A self-imposed constraint was that the metaclass mechanism must work without changing the already well-established class syntax."},{"id":"L-class-impl-problems","scope":"language","statement":"The original class implementation's problems became a frequent complaint among expert users: built-in types could not be subclassed, and the type system treated instances of unrelated classes as the same type."},{"id":"L-classes-afterthought","scope":"other","statement":"Adding classes to Python was essentially an afterthought, implemented in the 'cut corners' philosophy."},{"id":"L-new-style-coexist","scope":"language","statement":"New-style classes were introduced as a feature coexisting with old-style ones for backwards compatibility (old remaining the default in Python 2), created by subclassing an existing new-style class such as object, the root of the hierarchy; old-style classes will eventually be removed."},{"id":"L-metaclass-influence","scope":"other","statement":"The specific notion of metaclass came from the book 'Putting Metaclasses to Work' by Ira Forman and Scott Danforth, distinct from Smalltalk's similar concept."},{"id":"L-new-style-rewrite","scope":"language","statement":"In Python 2.2 Van Rossum reimplemented classes 'to do it right', the success."},{"id":"L-descriptor-classes","scope":"language","statement":"Python 2.2 added classmethod, staticmethod, and property as predefined classes built on the descriptor machinery."},{"id":"L-decorator-syntax","scope":"language","statement":"The @-decorator syntax (Python 2.4, derived from Java's annotations, decided by BDFL pronouncement) replaced successful features, exceeding expectations especially in web frameworks, and were extended to class definitions in Python 2.6."},{"id":"L-descriptors","scope":"language","statement":"Python 2.2 only wrapped Python functions (which blocked hybrid classes); the customization applies only in a class dictionary."},{"id":"L-new-method","scope":"language","statement":"__new__ was introduced as a immutable subclasses."},{"id":"L-new-style-concepts","scope":"language","statement":"New-style classes look similar to the original implementation on the surface but introduced __new__, descriptors, syntax because adding a major feature and new syntax at once was deemed too controversial, so users wrapped methods with extra assignment statements."},{"id":"L-slots","scope":"language","statement":"__slots__ is an application of descriptors that stores attributes in array slots and removes the instance __dict__; its real goal was standard library includes an easter-egg antigravity module referencing the XKCD comic, with a second hidden joke, a purported geohashing implementation, inside."},{"id":"L-mro-concept","scope":"language","statement":"The Method Resolution Order (MRO) is the order base classes are searched for a method, and in Python also for other attributes; it is interesting and subtle only under multiple inheritance."},{"id":"L-mro-diamond-problem","scope":"language","statement":"The classic depth-first, left-to-right search breaks under diamond inheritance by finding a shared ancestor's method instead of the more specialized override; since all new-style classes inherit from object, every use of multiple inheritance becomes a diamond, making this commonplace and the order critical."},{"id":"L-mro-22-broken","scope":"language","statement":"The MRO Van Rossum implemented for Python 2.2, with a special case reordering bases, diverged from the class."},{"id":"L-c3-adoption","scope":"language","statement":"Python adopted the C3 Linearization algorithm from the Dylan paper, which writes down all ordering rules imposed by inheritance and finds a monotonic ordering satisfying them all or fails."},{"id":"L-c3-rejects","scope":"language","statement":"C3 makes Python reject any inheritance hierarchy with an inconsistent ordering of base classes parentheses."},{"id":"L-list-comprehension","scope":"language","statement":"A list comprehension produces a list of a sequence's values selected by an optional predicate and mapped by a function, a L-abc-design-method.statement: ABC was designed by first doing a task analysis and then iterating with serious user testing.

L-abc-mixed-checking.statement: ABC used dynamic type checking for global variables and static for locals (locals dynamically checked too, to simplify implementation).

L-abc-runtime-checking.statement: ABC also re-checked argument types at run time, as a sanity check for its compiler and for readable error messages, needed because ABC is interactive.

L-abc-static-typed.statement: ABC was statically typed, rejecting inconsistent programs, using type inference rather than explicit declarations.

L-antigravity-easteregg.statement: Python 3's standard library includes an easter-egg antigravity module referencing the XKCD comic, with a second hidden joke, a purported geohashing implementation, inside.

L-assignment-instance-bootstrap.statement: Assignment can't default to an existing instance variable because of a bootstrap problem: there would be no way to create an instance variable the first time.

L-assignment-no-search.statement: Variable reference searches locals, globals, built-ins in order, but assignment never searches: it creates or replaces in the first (local) dictionary, with a global declaration the only override.

L-beaudry-hook.statement: Don Beaudry's insight that custom kinds of class objects should be creatable led to a hook: a callable type used as a base class makes class creation call that type, letting C (and later Python via a __class__ attribute) extensions define class behavior; it felt like a hack because type objects weren't yet callable, and it seeded metaclasses and new-style classes.

L-bool-type-history.statement: The bool type was formally introduced in Python 2.3 via PEP 285, with bool() and True/False backported into the 2.2.1 bugfix release (where they were a function and plain ints) to ease backporting of 2.3 code.

L-borrow-fix-abc.statement: The design program for Python was to keep what he liked from ABC while fixing its perceived problems, designing his own language rather than porting one.

L-bound-unbound-methods.statement: Calling a.spam() is a lookup returning a bound-method wrapper that stores the instance, then a call; bound and unbound methods share one internal type, and unbound methods were removed in Python 3000.

L-bridge-c-shell.statement: Python's original motivation was the need for a higher-level language to bridge the gap between C and the shell.

L-builtins-reassignable.statement: Built-in names are ordinary identifiers the parser gives no special knowledge, looked up at run time and freely reassignable, so adding a new built-in never invalidates code that used that name.

L-c-extensions-easy.statement: Python's implementation architecture made writing extension modules in C easy from the start.

L-c3-adoption.statement: Python adopted the C3 Linearization algorithm from the Dylan paper, which writes down all ordering rules imposed by inheritance and finds a monotonic ordering satisfying them all or fails.

L-c3-rejects.statement: C3 makes Python reject any inheritance hierarchy with an inconsistent ordering of base classes rather than resolving it silently, matching the Zen of Python's rule that errors should never pass silently.

L-class-attr-defaults.statement: Non-function class attributes serve as default values for instance variables: assignment to the instance shadows the class value and deletion reveals it again.

L-class-body-statements.statement: Any valid Python statements may appear in a class body, extending from allowing variable assignments to allowing arbitrary executable code.

L-class-callable-factory.statement: The class object itself is callable for instantiation, the minimal solution requiring no new syntax, making each class its own factory.

L-class-creation-api.statement: Defining a class executes its body in a local dictionary, then calls a class creation function with the name, a tuple of base classes, and that dictionary; originally internal, it became a public API and carried over unchanged into the Python 2.2 metaclass machinery.

L-class-creation-hidden.statement: In Python's original design classes were first-class objects, yet the act of creating a class was a fixed step hidden from users as an implementation detail.

L-class-dictionary.statement: The class object holds what is shared across instances in a class dictionary keyed by name; any object there (not just methods) becomes a class variable.

L-class-dynamic-modification.statement: Classes and instances can be modified dynamically by updating their dictionaries, though new-style classes require attribute assignment rather than using __dict__ directly.

L-class-exceptions-introduced.statement: Class exceptions were introduced in Python 1.5 (1997) and became the recommended, modern approach, with string exceptions later removed.

L-class-impl-problems.statement: The original class implementation's problems became a frequent complaint among expert users: built-in types could not be subclassed, and the type system treated instances of unrelated classes as the same type.

L-classbody-namespace-mechanism.statement: The class body is executed as statements in a new namespace whose resulting dictionary of locals initializes the class dictionary.

L-classes-added-late.statement: Classes were added late in Python's first year at CWI, but before the first public release.

L-classes-afterthought.statement: Adding classes to Python was essentially an afterthought, implemented in the 'cut corners' philosophy.

L-closures.statement: Inner functions should implicitly carry references to the enclosing scope's referenced local variables (closures); lambda originally couldn't, needing default-argument workarounds, and closures were added in 2.1/2.2, proving useful for new-style classes and decorators.

L-colon.statement: The colon separating the lead-in clause from the indented block, invented by ABC's authors, was kept because user testing showed it clarifies the indentation for beginners.

L-common-c-struct.statement: All Python objects are based on one common C data structure used everywhere in the interpreter, which made first-class-everything simple.

L-comprehension-design-factors.statement: Four factors governed the design of these notations: backwards compatibility, avoiding ambiguity, the desire for equivalence, and evolution of the language.

L-comprehension-extensions.statement: Python 3 added set and dict comprehensions as straightforward extensions of the list comprehension idea.

L-comprehension-forloop-origin.statement: The bare comma-separated values after 'in' recall Algol-60's for-loop, and since a colon always followed there was no ambiguity, so looping over known values shouldn't require parentheses.

L-comprehension-performance.statement: List comprehensions run faster than map plus lambda because a lambda call creates a new stack frame while the comprehension's expression is evaluated without one.

L-comprehension-vs-mapfilter.statement: List comprehensions are an alternative to map() and filter() that wins on realistic cases, and Van Rossum finds them more readable than the functional notation as complexity grows, rejecting the view that a terser lambda would fix map().

L-concise.statement: Seemingly complicated tasks can often be expressed in very little Python code.

L-constant-convention.statement: A constant such as an all-caps identifier is only a convention the parser neither knows nor enforces, distinct from a literal.

L-decorator-syntax.statement: The @-decorator syntax (Python 2.4, derived from Java's annotations, decided by BDFL pronouncement) replaced wrapping-by-assignment, which had forced the reader to the end of a method to learn its kind.

L-decorators-success.statement: Decorators became one of the most successful features, exceeding expectations especially in web frameworks, and were extended to class definitions in Python 2.6.

L-descriptor-classes.statement: Python 2.2 added classmethod, staticmethod, and property as predefined classes built on the descriptor machinery.

L-descriptor-no-syntax.statement: Descriptors were introduced without new syntax because adding a major feature and new syntax at once was deemed too controversial, so users wrapped methods with extra assignment statements.

L-descriptors.statement: Python 2.2 generalized method wrapping into descriptors: the object found by attribute search decides via __get__ (and __set__/__delete__) what get, set, and delete mean, replacing the hard-coded scheme that only wrapped Python functions (which blocked hybrid classes); the customization applies only in a class dictionary.

L-dict-based-lookup.statement: Attribute access is plain dictionary operations: setting updates the instance dictionary; lookup checks the instance dictionary, then the class, then the base classes.

L-distinguish-exceptions.statement: Making exceptions work requires some scheme for distinguishing one kind of exception from another.

L-distutils.statement: The distutils tool let users build and install extension modules from anywhere and became a standard library module, but its complexity and lack of maintenance led to third-party alternatives and community fragmentation.

L-dynamic-loading.statement: Python's import was interfaced with each platform's dynamic linking API so extension modules could be compiled and loaded separately as shared libraries, replacing early static linking into the interpreter and creating a cross-platform maintenance burden.

L-dynamic-no-return.statement: Once dynamic typing is chosen there is no going back, because in Python a type cannot be deduced from the form of an operation (x+y is ambiguous), unlike ABC's operations.

L-dynamic-typing.statement: Python is dynamically typed: variables are names referring to objects, need no declaration, and all type checking happens at run time.

L-embedding.statement: Users asked for an embeddable Python, a library linkable into other applications, as Emacs embeds a Lisp interpreter.

L-everything-statement.statement: Every part of the language is an executable statement that can appear anywhere, which simplified the grammar (earlier it restricted declarative constructs to the top level).

L-exception-identity-nameclash.statement: Exceptions were given identity semantics (distinct string objects are distinct exceptions, referenced by name not value) to avoid name clashes across modules, influenced by Modula-3's unique exception tokens and predating string interning.

L-exception-pointer-optimization.statement: He wanted to test exceptions by pointer comparison rather than string value, a misguided premature optimization of execution time.

L-exceptions-as-strings.statement: Early Python identified exceptions by strings, an unfortunate choice made because a new built-in type would cost much C coding and strings carry error messages.

L-exceptions-errorhandling.statement: Python handles errors through exceptions, raised and caught with try/except/finally.

L-first-class.statement: Every object that can be named in Python is first class, with equal status: assignable, passable, storable in data structures.

L-floor-division.statement: Python's integer division returns the floor, rounding toward negative infinity rather than truncating toward zero like C, matching number theory's preferred convention and paired with modulo to satisfy a mathematical relationship, with a worry about extending the floor rule to floating-point modulo.

L-for-iterable.statement: Python's for statement loops over any iterable object rather than over a numeric index.

L-functional-added.statement: In January 1994 map(), filter(), reduce(), and the lambda operator for anonymous functions were added, a significant early chunk of contributed code.

L-functional-superseded.statement: The map, filter, and reduce functions were largely superseded by list comprehensions and generator expressions; reduce was removed from the built-ins in Python 3 while lambda, map and filter stay.

L-general-purpose.statement: Python is a general purpose language in the lineage of Lisp or Smalltalk, not merely a scripting language.

L-genexp.statement: Generator expressions, added in 2.4 and enabled by generators, represent a sequence of results without building a concrete list, saving memory, running in a separate frame so they don't leak the variable but were less efficient than list comprehensions in Python 2.

L-genexp-syntax.statement: A generator expression's parentheses belong to the surrounding call, so a bare comma sequence after 'in' would be ambiguous; Python required a single expression there, unlike Python 2 list comprehensions, choosing not to guess and not to break existing list-comprehension code.

L-grammar-overpermissive.statement: The grammar accepted constructs the semantics didn't support, such as nested functions without nested scopes, which worked in broken ways until later fixed.

L-grand-renaming.statement: The Py-prefix rename, a traumatic kind of event for developer communities, was done in two phases bridged by preprocessor macros for backwards compatibility, accompanied by adding unit tests to much of the standard library.

L-halfopen-slicing-indexing.statement: Python chose 0-based indexing with half-open slice intervals and suitable defaults, so common slicing cases (first n items, next n from i) come out as a[:n] and a[i:i+n] without +1/-1 corrections.

L-handwritten-lexer.statement: Van Rossum chose not to use a lexer generator, writing the lexer by hand, because the Lex he knew would segfault on long tokens and he figured indentation would be hard to teach a generator.

L-hashtable.statement: He replaced ABC's sorted-table (B-tree) mapping with a hash table, as faster and easier to implement.

L-immutable-primitives.statement: Python's primitive built-in types (Booleans, numbers, strings) are immutable.

L-impl-bytecode.statement: Python is implemented as a bytecode compiler plus a stack-based interpreter written in C, with compilation done implicitly as modules load.

L-indentation.statement: Python groups statements by indentation instead of braces, an idea taken from ABC that predates it.

L-instance-representation.statement: An instance is the simplest possible design: a built-in object holding a class reference and an instance dictionary.

L-int-float-silent-error.statement: Because Python has no type declarations, passing an integer where a float is expected is not caught and yields an answer with a much larger error, hard to debug.

L-int-long-different-semantics.statement: Machine ints and longs had slightly different semantics: ints clipped on overflow and were treated as unsigned by bitwise/shift/conversion, longs always signed.

L-integer-division.statement: Python's truncating integer division, departing from ABC's exact rationals, was an early mistake with large consequences, fixed with //, a future import, and a flag, becoming default in Python 3000 despite opposition.

L-introspection-type-object.statement: Python's introspection comes from making the type structure itself available at run time as an object like any other.

L-keyword-definition.statement: A keyword (reserved word) looks like an identifier but the parser treats it as a token of the language, and so it can never be used to name a variable, function, or class.

L-keywords-costly.statement: Every reserved word must be known by everyone using Python since it can never be a name, so the list is kept small and many proposed features were killed or changed to avoid needing a new keyword.

L-lalr-regret.statement: In hindsight Van Rossum might choose a more powerful LALR(1) parsing engine, since several grammar areas (e.g. keyword arguments) need more power than LL(1).

L-lambda-intent.statement: Lambda was intended only as a syntactic tool for defining anonymous functions, not a full functional construct.

L-lambda-motivation.statement: Users wanted a way to create anonymous functions in-line rather than defining a separate named function (as Lisp and Scheme allow), since Python had no such mechanism despite first-class functions, and the exec-string workaround was hacky.

L-lambda-terminology.statement: The 'lambda' terminology, adopted for lack of a better alternative despite Van Rossum's unease, led functional-language users to expect semantics and advanced features Python lacked.

L-less-discussion-early.statement: In the early days big changes required much less discussion than later, for better and worse.

L-list-comprehension.statement: A list comprehension produces a list of a sequence's values selected by an optional predicate and mapped by a function, a Pythonic interpretation of the mathematical set-builder notation, with multiple for-clauses allowed for nested loops.

L-list-flexible-array.statement: He changed ABC's sorted-bag list into a flexible array with insert/delete, giving users full control of ordering, with a sort method.

L-listcomp-genexp-equivalence.statement: In Python 3 a list comprehension was made fully equivalent to list() applied to the corresponding generator expression, so it was given the stricter genexp syntax.

L-listcomp-leak.statement: Python 2 list comprehensions leaked the loop control variable into the surrounding scope, an intentional speed compromise; Python 3 fixed this by using the generator-expression implementation strategy, and with general speedups both forms became faster with no speed difference, removing the performance argument.

L-literal-definition.statement: A literal is an element of an expression describing a constant value, recognized by the parser and producing a different parse tree from a name, so the left-hand side of an assignment must be a variable and a literal is not one.

L-long-bignum.statement: He added an unbounded exact integer type, long, for the use case of arbitrary-precision numbers.

L-long-suffix-violation.statement: Requiring a trailing L to mark longs violated the ABC-inspired philosophy of not making users care about uninteresting implementation details.

L-machine-ints-common.statement: He did not want bignums for all integer operations: machine integers serve the common cases, bignums only serious math.

L-metaclass-influence.statement: The specific notion of metaclass came from the book 'Putting Metaclasses to Work' by Ira Forman and Scott Danforth, distinct from Smalltalk's similar concept.

L-metaclass-namespace-limit.statement: The class body is executed before the class creation function runs, so a metaclass could not influence the namespace the definitions run in; Python 3000 fixed this by letting a metaclass provide an alternative mapping, specified with keyword-argument syntax in the base-class list.

L-metaclass-no-syntax-change.statement: A self-imposed constraint was that the metaclass mechanism must work without changing the already well-established class syntax.

L-metaclass-not-ruby.statement: Python's metaclass design did not come from Ruby.

L-method-resolution-mro.statement: Method resolution walks the class then each base recursively, the depth-first, left-to-right rule, the default MRO in most versions.

L-mixed-mode-arithmetic.statement: He initially forbade mixed-mode arithmetic to keep type implementations independent, until Tim Peters convinced him to add it with the usual coercion rules.

L-modula3-method-model.statement: The self approach, and Python's import and exception syntax, resemble Modula-3, where x.m(args) equals f(x,args).

L-mro-22-algorithm.statement: For Python 2.2 the MRO was pre-computed at class-definition time and stored as a class attribute, dropping all but the last occurrence of a duplicated class.

L-mro-22-broken.statement: The MRO Van Rossum implemented for Python 2.2, with a special case reordering bases, diverged from the simpler algorithm he documented, and Samuele Pedroni found inconsistencies violating monotonicity, so it was judged broken, a regret.

L-mro-concept.statement: The Method Resolution Order (MRO) is the order base classes are searched for a method, and in Python also for other attributes; it is interesting and subtle only under multiple inheritance.

L-mro-diamond-problem.statement: The classic depth-first, left-to-right search breaks under diamond inheritance by finding a shared ancestor's method instead of the more specialized override; since all new-style classes inherit from object, every use of multiple inheritance becomes a diamond, making this commonplace and the order critical.

L-mro-three-algorithms.statement: Python has used three MRO algorithms over time (classic, 2.2 new-style, and 2.3 new-style / C3), of which only C3 survives in Python 3.

L-multiple-impls.statement: Besides the C reference implementation, Python has several other implementations (Jython on the JVM, IronPython on .NET, PyPy, Stackless).

L-multiple-inheritance.statement: Class objects hold references to one or more base classes, supporting a simple-minded multiple inheritance.

L-name-python.statement: The name Python was chosen under-analyzed as irreverent, fitting the tradition of naming languages after people, and only later associated with snakes.

L-new-method.statement: __new__ was introduced as a class method hook for customizing instance creation, which old-style classes lacked, enabling patterns like Singleton, returning existing or different-class instances, use in pickle, and initializing immutable subclasses.

L-new-style-coexist.statement: New-style classes were introduced as a feature coexisting with old-style ones for backwards compatibility (old remaining the default in Python 2), created by subclassing an existing new-style class such as object, the root of the hierarchy; old-style classes will eventually be removed.

L-new-style-concepts.statement: New-style classes look similar to the original implementation on the surface but introduced __new__, descriptors, static and class methods, properties, decorators, slots, and a new Method Resolution Order.

L-new-style-rewrite.statement: In Python 2.2 Van Rossum reimplemented classes 'to do it right', the most ambitious subsystem rewrite to date (risking second-system syndrome), adding subclassable built-in types, true metaclasses, a fixed MRO and more, and it proved a major success.

L-newstyle-iteration.statement: New-style classes were only the second or third iteration of the metaclass idea, which Van Rossum had already written about in 1998.

L-no-feature-in-bugfix.statement: Adding a new feature in a bugfix release (bool in 2.2.1) was the most criticized such instance and would not be done now.

L-no-method-checking.statement: Method lookup does no error or conformance checking: an override need not match the base method's arguments, and the first method found is called.

L-no-separate-method-syntax.statement: A major constraint was not to add a method-definition syntax different from the function syntax.

L-no-undefined-raise.statement: There are no undefined result values in Python: an exception is always raised when no correct value can be computed.

L-none-keyword.statement: None was eventually made a reserved word for mostly social reasons (its centrality, users horrified that assignment to it was allowed), with minor benefits in speed and catching typos and no downside since nothing assigns to it.

L-none-singleton.statement: None is a singleton object used throughout the language and library to represent the absence of some other value.

L-none-true-false-both.statement: None, True and False are both keywords (how the parser recognizes them) and literals (their role standing for constant values in expressions).

L-not-functional.statement: Van Rossum never viewed Python as a functional language or heavily influenced by them, and its dynamic nature rules out functional-style compile-time optimization such as tail recursion.

L-object-type-struct.statement: An object type is a statically allocated structure of function pointers, one per standard operation, with optional ones left NULL.

L-oop-support.statement: Python has full object-oriented support: user-defined classes, inheritance, and run-time binding of methods.

L-open-source-early.statement: Python's first public release used an MIT-style license, so it was open source before the term was coined.

L-overflow-check.statement: Integer operations check for overflow and raise OverflowError rather than silently clipping; in hindsight they should instead promote the result to long.

L-own-parser-generator.statement: Van Rossum wrote his own LL(1) parser generator because the landscape of parser generators was sparse, he disliked Yacc, and he was unfamiliar with or distrusted more advanced techniques as too inefficient.

L-permissive-vs-smalltalk.statement: Python's objects are more permissive than Smalltalk's, which restricts an object's attributes to those fixed at creation.

L-pgen.statement: The first code written for Python was a simple LL(1) parser generator, pgen, still in the distribution and the least changed.

L-pgen2.statement: A Python rewrite of pgen (pgen2, under lib2to3) was created at Elemental Security with an input format identical to the original, was used for 2to3, and in Python 3.8 replaced the C pgen.

L-py-prefix.statement: A naming convention was adopted prefixing all Python C globals with Py, _Py for internal names, and PY for macros, to avoid clashes.

L-python-like-lisp.statement: Python has much in common with Lisp in deep structure despite being completely different at the surface syntactic level.

L-python-origins-cwi.statement: Python grew from experience at CWI: ABC gave the inspiration, Amoeba the motivation, the multimedia group its growth.

L-rationals-failed.statement: ABC's exact rational numbers didn't pan out: programs silently ran on numbers with thousands of digits, slow, and the fix was non-intuitive for beginners.

L-regex-ebnf-grammar.statement: pgen used regular-expression (EBNF) notation instead of standard BNF to make the grammar easier to read and resolve conflicts without awkwardly named helper rules, without changing the LL(1) power, with parse-tree nodes of variable arity and tables derived by regex->NFA->DFA.

L-reject-instancevar-declarations.statement: Explicit instance-variable declarations were rejected (he had gotten this far with none), and lexical markers like a sigil did not appeal to him.

L-releases-cvs.statement: Encouraged by feedback, he kept a steady stream of releases and adopted CVS to track changes and share coding.

L-repr-valid-input.statement: Every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression valid as input to the parser (a rule from ABC).

L-result-type-rule.statement: The major mistake was borrowing C's rule that an arithmetic operation's result is always the same type as its operands, which makes sense in C but not in a very-high-level language.

L-ruby-inspired-by-python.statement: Ruby was inspired by Python; Matz told Van Rossum his inspiration was 20% Python, 80% Perl, with Larry Wall as his hero.

L-self-explicit.statement: A method is just a function whose first argument, named self by convention, is the instance; explicit reference is the only way to reach instance variables, since implicit C++-style resolution is impossible without declarations.

L-sequence-concept.statement: List, tuple, and string were generalized to a common sequence concept so length, indexing, slicing, and iteration work the same on any of them.

L-setbuilder-difference.statement: Mathematical set-builder notation implies a universal set understood from context; Python has no universal set and, in Python 2.0, no sets at all, which forced a different notation.

L-siebren-classes-suggestion.statement: Siebren van der Zee first suggested Python allow C++-like class definitions so objects could be implemented in Python, not only C.

L-slots.statement: __slots__ is an application of descriptors that stores attributes in array slots and removes the instance __dict__; its real goal was performance (a fallback against a feared attribute-access slowdown), not attribute-name safety.

L-smalltalk-bytecode-influence.statement: Smalltalk's bytecode, which Van Rossum read about in a book by Adele Goldberg and others, was a bigger influence on Python's bytecode.

L-smalltalk-metaclass-unaware.statement: Van Rossum was only vaguely aware of Smalltalk at the time and was surprised, reading about it much later, by its use of metaclasses, which differs from Python's or Ruby's.

L-special-methods.statement: Special behaviors (initializers, destructors, operators) are handled by methods with special underscore names mapped to the C function-pointer tables, rather than new syntax.

L-standalone-globals.statement: Python was first conceived as a stand-alone program, so its C source freely defined global linker names without namespace discipline, which clashed with host applications when embedding.

L-stdlib.statement: Python's extensive, always-evolving standard library is one of the main reasons for its popularity.

L-string-literal-unification-bug.statement: The bytecode compiler unified string literals within a module, so exceptions could accidentally be caught by their message, which broke across modules and caused confusion.

L-syntax-from-c.statement: Python's surface syntax borrows heavily from C in keywords, naming rules, and operators.

L-syntax-tastes.statement: His tastes in syntax were strongly influenced by Algol 60, Pascal, Algol 68, and ABC.

L-traditional-number-model.statement: Python chose a traditional numeric model of machine integers (C long) and binary floating point (C double) plus an arbitrary-precision long, rather than ABC's rationals.

L-true-false-keywords.statement: True and False were first introduced as built-in constants rather than keywords to keep backward compatibility with code defining its own, then made keywords in Python 3 by analogy to None.

L-tuple-from-abc.statement: He kept ABC's immutable tuple with packing and unpacking, adding array-like indexing and slicing.

L-tuple-syntax.statement: A trailing comma makes a one-tuple and "()" the empty tuple, so representations remain valid parser input.

L-type-is-object.statement: From its original 1990 design Python made 'type' itself an object: every object's type pointer points to a special object of C function pointers (like a C++ vtable), and a type's own type is a special meta-type recognized by being its own type.

L-why-not-shell.statement: The Bourne shell wouldn't do because Amoeba's primitive operations were finer-grained and different from the shell's.
